cards.title: hacer = to do / to make
cards.body: Silent h; the c sounds like s (th in much of Spain). Each time you meet a new verb, note its type: hacer is an -er verb, so it uses e.

cards.title: qué = what
cards.body: ¿Qué haces? means 'what are you doing?' and is also a casual 'how are you? / what are you up to?'. The -s (informal you) and -n (they / you all) endings appear throughout Spanish verbs.

cards.title: Remembering ≠ memorising
cards.body: You do need to remember Spanish, but forced memorising blocks it. Using the language from many angles while building sentences makes it truly yours rather than borrowed.

cards.title: puedo = I can (poder)
cards.body: An -er verb. A d between vowels is soft. Spanish keeps the 'to' idea after it: puedes venir = 'can you (to) come'. The informal -s is the same as in ¿cómo estás?

examples.en: I want to know why you can't come.
examples.es: Quiero saber por qué no puedes venir.

cards.title: More verbs for the I form
salgo — another -go verb
cards.body: Salir (to leave, go out) gives salgo, not 'salo', like tengo and vengo. Common verbs tend to be the irregular ones in any language.

cards.title: esperar = to wait / to hope
cards.body: Waiting and hoping share one verb. English 'desperate' (des- = un-) contains it: without hope.

cards.title: Check the verb type first
cards.body: The e sounds in espe- tempt you to say 'espere'. Before changing a verb, go back to the 'to' form (esperar → -ar) and take control: espera.

examples.en: I want to know why they're not waiting for me.
examples.es: Quiero saber por qué no me esperan.

cards.title: v ↔ b, and -ary → -ario
cards.body: V and b shift between languages: vocabulario comes from boca (mouth). English -ary becomes -ario.

practice.why: hacer → hacen; lo before the verb.

practice.en: I want to know why they're not waiting for me.
es: Quiero saber por qué no me esperan
Quiero saber porque no me esperan
practice.why: quiero saber + por qué + no me esperan.
